decisions.quote:
Study 1 was a direct replication of previous cross-cultural research on the religiosity-

adjustment relation. Yet, this study differed from previous research in three important ways.

First, previous research operationalized psychological adjustment as life satisfaction

(Stavrova et al., 2013), subjective well-being (Diener et al., 2011), depression (Leurent et al.,

2013), or social self-esteem (Gebauer et al., 2012b). From an RASV perspective, however,

global self-esteem is the most appropriate adjustment indicator.

Re-testing this cross-cultural moderation with global self-esteem (and also testing the Gallup World Poll country-level religiosity index in Note 10 and interpersonal-contact controls in Study 3) is an explicit conceptual replication. Diener et al. (2011) is completely distinct from shipped row 405 (Gebauer et al., 2013d / corrected to Gebauer, Sedikides, & Neberich, 2012b) and sibling targets 2 and 3.
